How many rental units to own, and why the last one rarely pays

Every rental business that owns identical units, whether party tents, kayaks, scaffold sets or camera bodies, faces the same quiet decision each time it buys one. Too few and the busiest days turn customers away. Too many and units sit in the shed earning nothing while their insurance, storage and depreciation run. The honest way to see the trade-off is a curve: the yearly profit of owning one unit, two, three and so on. It rises, peaks and falls, and the peak is where to stop.

Open the free fleet size optimizer

Why each extra unit earns less

The first unit is out almost every day there is a request. The tenth is only needed on the days when nine others are already out. Those days are few, so the tenth unit is rented a handful of times a year, while it costs exactly as much to own as the first. Demand also comes in seasons, which makes it worse: a fleet sized for the summer peak is mostly idle in the off-season. The useful number is the extra profit of the next unit, and the right fleet is the largest one whose next unit still earns more than it costs.

A worked example

An invented party-tent business gets 2.4 rental requests a day for 150 peak days, 1 a day for 61 shoulder days and 0.15 a day for the 154 days of off-season. Rentals last one day (25 percent of them), two (45), three (20) or seven (10), an average of 2.45 days. It charges $85 per tent per day, spends $18 on cleaning and delivery per rental, and each tent costs $1,100 a year to own. All of these figures are invented for the example. Treating bookings as arriving at any hour, the Erlang loss formula gives:

TentsTurned awayProfit per yearThis tent adds
621.1%$60,021$5,902
89.4%$67,764$3,219
103.2%$70,779$994
111.7%$70,972$192
120.8%$70,602−$370

The sixth tent adds $5,902 a year. The eleventh adds $192, and the twelfth costs $370 more than it brings in, so the best fleet is 11 tents. Notice how little is at stake near the top: the profit at 10, 11 and 12 tents is within about $400 a year, so the choice among them can safely be made on things the model does not see, such as your cash or your storage space. Notice also what a unit must earn: at $85 less $7 of per-rental cost spread over the average rental, a tent needs about 15 rental days a year (14.2, rounded up) to cover its $1,100.

If the same business books by calendar date, so that a tent returned on Friday can go out again on Friday, a simulation of 200 years gives a slightly lower best fleet of 10 tents, because fewer requests are turned away at every size. The tool computes both and uses the one that matches how you book.

Finding your own stopping point

  1. Write down your seasons, how many days each lasts, and how many rental requests a day you get in each. Count the requests you turned away too.
  2. List how long rentals last and what share of rentals are each length.
  3. Put a yearly figure on owning one unit: depreciation or finance, storage, insurance, upkeep.
  4. Read the curve and stop where the next unit adds less than zero.
  5. Check the demand table: if 15 percent less demand moves the answer by one unit, you have room; if it moves it by three, be careful.

The optimizer does steps 4 and 5, and it also shows what a bad year (one in ten) looks like and what a limit on turned-away customers would cost.

Common questions

Should I own enough units for my busiest weekend?

Only if a unit earns its yearly cost on the days it is out. A unit bought for the busiest weekend is rented only on the few days when everything else is already rented, so it needs a very high rate on those days to cover twelve months of owning it. Work out the rental days a unit needs in a year to break even, then compare it with how many days the last unit would really be out.

Does the average rental length or the mix of lengths matter more?

For the any-hour model only the average matters. For the day-by-day model the mix matters a little, because many short rentals free units sooner than a few long ones, but the average is still what drives how many units are out at once. Enter your real mix if you know it and a single average if you do not.

Why does a unit that is rented 40 percent of the time still lose money?

Utilisation is not profit. A unit that is out 146 days a year at a margin of about $78 a day earns about $11,300, so it pays a $1,100 owning cost many times over. A unit out 10 days earns about $780 and does not. The tool compares the days the next unit would add with the days it needs.

Pricing a single rental rather than sizing the fleet? The bounce house rental calculator prices one rental job and shows what it earns.

RENTAL FLEET SIZE OPTIMIZER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

How many units should you own?

Enter your seasons of demand, how long rentals last, what you charge and what a unit costs to own. The tool computes the yearly profit of every fleet size two ways, with the Erlang loss formula and a repeatable day-by-day simulation, then recommends how many units to own, how many customers that turns away, what a bad year looks like and how the answer moves if demand does.

Arithmetic and simulation on figures you supply. Not legal, tax, or financial advice. New to this? Read how many rental units to own, and why the last one rarely pays.

Demand by season

Count requests, including the ones you turned away. Weekends can be their own season. Days should add up to about 365.

How long rentals last

Shares can be counts or percentages. A single number means every rental is that long.

Money

The cost of owning a unit is what it costs you whether or not it is out: depreciation or finance, storage, insurance, upkeep.

How bookings arrive

Add your seasons and rental lengths, then click Find the best fleet size.

How it is calculated

Offered load: requests per day times the average rental length, in units. Erlang B: with c units and offered load a, the share of requests turned away is B(c) from B(0) = 1 and B(c) = a·B(c−1) / (c + a·B(c−1)). It depends only on the average rental length, not on how lengths vary. Each season is computed on its own and summed, because the fleet is fixed while demand is not. Day-by-day simulation: each day draws a number of requests (Poisson, or negative binomial when clustering is above 1), each request draws a rental length from your mix and takes a free unit or is turned away. Units come back on the day after the last rental day and can go out again that day. Every fleet size sees the same simulated years from a fixed seed, one warm-up year is discarded, and the table shows the mean year and the 10th-percentile year. Profit: price × rental days − cost per rental × rentals − cost of turning a customer away × turn-aways − units × yearly cost of owning one. Recommendation: the fleet size with the highest mean profit, or the smallest size meeting your turn-away limit if that is larger. Calendar-booked rentals use the simulation; any-hour rentals use Erlang B.

Not modelled: different unit types, damage, theft or units out for repair, deposits, delivery routes and staff, taxes and financing, resale value, waiting lists or customers who come back later, and rentals that cross the year boundary (revenue is counted when a rental starts). Unverified: tested against hand-calculated Erlang values, an exact one-day-rental formula and a repeatable simulation, not on a real rental business's books. It does not tell you what to charge or which unit to buy.

Common questions

How many units should a small rental business own?

As many as still pay for themselves. Each extra unit rescues fewer requests than the one before it, because it is only needed on the few busiest days, while it costs the same to own every day of the year. The table in this tool shows the yearly profit of every fleet size from one upward and marks the size after which the next unit earns less than it costs to own.

Why not just buy enough for the busiest weekend?

Because the busiest weekend is a handful of days and the unit sits in the shed for the rest of the year. A unit needs a minimum number of rental days a year to cover its cost; the tool prints that number from your own price and costs. When the last unit you are considering would be out fewer days than that, it loses money even though every request in the peak would have been served.

What is the difference between Erlang B and the day-by-day simulation?

Erlang B is the classic formula for the share of requests turned away when every unit is busy. It assumes requests arrive at any moment and a unit is only free once it is back. The simulation books by calendar day, so a unit returned on a day can go out again that day, and it can model bookings that cluster. Calendar-booked rentals such as a tent for Saturday sit closer to the simulation; hourly or walk-up rentals sit closer to Erlang B. The tool computes both and lets you choose which drives the recommendation.

What does the booking clustering setting do?

It sets how much busier and quieter than average the days are, as a variance-to-mean ratio. At 1, requests arrive independently. At 2 or 3, a day's requests swing more widely around the average, as they do when weather, holidays or a single event drive bookings. Clustering turns away more customers at the same fleet size, so the best fleet and the bad-year figures both move.

Can I set a limit on how many customers I turn away?

Yes. Enter the largest share of requests you are willing to turn away, and the recommendation becomes the larger of the most profitable fleet and the smallest fleet that meets the limit. The result says what the limit costs you in a year, so you can see the price of the promise before making it.

What does it not model?

It treats the units as identical and the demand as figures you type. It does not model different unit types, damage or theft, units out of service for repair, deposits, delivery routing, staff, taxes, financing or the resale value of a unit. The yearly cost of owning a unit is a number you supply, so include depreciation, storage, insurance and upkeep in it.

Is my data uploaded?

No. Everything runs in your browser from the figures you type, nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and it works offline after the page loads.
